item.title: When the rain, the runoff, and the tide arrive together. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B

On the night of July 4, 2025, the Guadalupe River in Texas Hill Country rose about 26 feet in 45 minutes. Camp Mystic, a girls' summer camp on its banks, lost 27 campers, counselors, and its director before dawn. More than 135 people died across the region in that single flood, according to state investigative findings. What made the event so lethal was not simply how much rain fell. The National Weather Service's own warnings that night cited rainfall rates climbing to several inches an hour, a pace that turned a river into a wall of water before most people even understood a flood was underway. This is the point that gets lost in most conversations about flooding, in Texas and in Bangladesh alike. The number that matters most in the changing climate is often not the total rainfall for the day, but how fast it arrives. A given volume of rain spread over 12 hours is manageable. The same volume in 90 minutes can be fatal. Chittagong found this out on its own terms this July, when the city recorded about 410 millimetres of rain in 24 hours, according to a Dhaka Tribune report, the heaviest single-day total the port city had seen in 42 years. The rain fell hardest while the Karnaphuli River was at high tide, and while runoff from the surrounding hills poured into a drainage network already at its limit. A city I did not expect to see this in I grew up in Comilla, and waterlogging is not something I remember from my childhood there. A hard rain meant wet streets that dried out again by the next day. That is no longer true. Comilla now floods most summers, sometimes badly enough that students have had to reach their exam centres by boat. Comilla has no hills to cut and no tide to fight. What it has, like dozens of other urbanizing cities across Bangladesh and beyond, is a much less dramatic but equally potent sequence: Canal margins and low channels lost to construction, drains left uncleared for years, and a habit, shared by households, markets, and construction sites alike, of treating the nearest drain as the easiest place to get rid of waste. None of that needed a hill or a coastline. It only needed disregard for the environment and indifferent authorities. Two cities, two different problems Dhaka and Chittagong show the same underlying pattern at a larger, more studied scale, each with its own mechanism layered on top. Dhaka's story is mostly about disappearing land. According to a study on canal encroachment in Dhaka, the city has lost roughly 60% of its wetlands and 65% of its canals over the past 30 years, paved over as construction spread. Retention ponds that once held monsoon runoff have shrunk sharply in the areas where records exist. That is a loss of natural capacity to absorb water, separate from anything happening in the pipes. The piped network is its own weak point. A Daily Star investigation found that Dhaka's main drainage authority maintains roughly 370 kilometres of storm drainage pipe, covering only about a fifth of the city's 400 square kilometre area, with seven different agencies each looking after their own section and little coordination between them. So even where canals are intact, the underground system meant to feed them is often undersized, aging, or simply absent. Chittagong has, or used to have, a hilly terrain and sits next to a coastline, a perfect combination for compound flooding where bidirectional flow coming from the sea and the land overwhelms the natural and built drainage infrastructure. Chittagong has also historically seen heavier monsoon rain because of its proximity to the sea. When a hillside is cut for construction, it destroys a delicate hydrologic balance. As in Dhaka, loss of natural drainage to land grabbing compounds the strain on what remains of the natural drainage pattern. According to a 2023 Daily Star report, the city's own drainage authority now counts 56 canals where 72 once existed, and green space has fallen below 15% of the city's land. Underground drainage fares no better. A recent engineering study found that large parts of the city have no properly connected underground network at all, which means canal restoration alone will not solve the problem even where it succeeds. Underneath both cities' specific drivers of waterlogging sits a simpler failure that needs no special geography to operate: Neglect. Drains and canals that are not regularly cleared silt up regardless of how well they were designed, and clearing them depends on maintenance schedules and budgets that routinely lose out to flashier priorities. An ordinary afternoon shower is often enough to expose a canal that has not been desilted in years, or a drain choked with waste that residents and businesses put there themselves. This pattern is not confined to Dhaka and Chittagong, or even to Bangladesh. Wetlands, floodplains, and canal margins disappear first precisely because they look empty between storms. Each time this happens, in any city following the same sequence, the next flood has less capacity to work with than the one before it. Plans that stop keeping up Dhaka's current drainage plan, drafted by WASA in 2015, assumed 40% of rainfall would soak naturally into the ground, and its pumping stations were sized to match. That was a reasonable estimate at the time, according to an urban planner quoted in a July 2026 Daily Star report. As concrete replaced open soil across the city in the years since, actual infiltration fell well below that number, and the plan was never revised. The same report notes that the city's pumps can now handle only about 40% of the current load. Chittagong's plan is older and carries a different kind of stale assumption. Its Storm Water Drainage and Flood Control Master Plan was drafted between 1993 and 1995. One specific flaw stands out: According to a paper in the Journal of Bangladesh Institute of Planners, drain widths were fixed at 2 to 3 feet regardless of whether the road above them was 20 feet or 60 feet wide, so as development scaled up around them, the drains never did. Hill cutting, meanwhile, is banned under a separate national law, the Environment Conservation Act of 1995, but enforcement has been too weak to stop it. Spending has not been the constraint Chittagong's experience argues against the idea that money is the missing piece. According to a recent statement from the finance minister, four major flood-mitigation projects have been running for close to a decade, with roughly Tk 14,400 crore allocated and about Tk 10,400 crore of it already spent. A separate Daily Star report found that the largest single project, covering 36 canals, has seen its cost rise from about Tk 5,600 crore to roughly Tk 8,600 crore, with its deadline pushed from 2020 to 2026. Over that same period, according to the same report, the city has lost 47 of its original 104 canals to encroachment and sedimentation. Money spent building fixed infrastructure to an unrevised design, without enforcement, coordination, or updated assumptions behind it, buys less every year the city keeps changing. A bigger budget applied to the same static approach does not fix that problem. It just makes it more expensive. What this argues for None of this argues against having a master plan. It argues against treating one as a document written once and left alone for 20 years. A better version is a living plan: Built and updated at the scale of individual drainage basins, with lessons from each basin carried into the next. item.title: Spray and pray is not an export strategy. [ dawn ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B

Somewhere in Sialkot, a surgical instruments manufacturer is holding a purchase order from a distributor in Frankfurt.

Someone in Washington, DC, is still trying to figure out how to import mangoes from Pakistan without going through the hassle of asking relatives or going through an informal distribution chain, while some kid in Oslo wants to buy a Trionda (the official football of the FIFA World Cup 2026), but just doesn’t know where to get it officially.

The demand in these cases is real, the margins work, and the buyers are willing to pay a premium. The supplier is willing to ship directly, but it doesn’t know how to do the same, and because of this information asymmetry, its bank declines because it isn’t aware of who the buyer is, the working capital cycle does not fit any product on the shelf, and a multitude of other reasons.

Summer transitions to Fall, the orders detailed above lapse. Nothing in the national accounts records this event, yet it is precisely where Pakistan’s export stagnation lives.

Firms are 80pc more likely to qualify for support on traditional products than on new ones

The instinctive policy response to weak exports has always been to throw more money at the problem, but as the Notorious B.I.G once wrote, the more money we come across, the more problems we see. Another refinance line, another subsidy window, or another mark-up support scheme is the reflex response — there is no shortage of loanable funds, but there is a dearth of loanable funds for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which is compounded by a shortage of structures that convert commercially viable transactions into bankable ones.

It is estimated that the Export Finance Scheme reaches roughly five per cent of exporters, whereas long-term financing under the Long- Term Financing Facility (LT FF) reaches fewer than 1pc, in terms of number of exporters. The top 100 exporters, who account for about 40pc of export value, absorb twothirds of all export finance, and 86pc of LT FF flows into textiles and allied segments.

As per Gonzalo (2024) in “Evaluating the impact of export finance support on firm-level export performance: evidence from Pakistan”, the evaluated impact is real but narrow, as participants grow export volume by seven to 11 percentage points, with no statistically significant effect on the number of products exported or markets served.

Firms are 80pc more likely to qualify for support on traditional products than on new ones. In effect, we finance more of what we already sell, to buyers we already know. Such schemes only finance scale, but do not finance discovery.

The structural arithmetic shows what this has cost us. The average Pakistani exporter ships $1.4 million a year, one-third of Bangladesh’s $3.8m. The median exporter ships just $68,000. Only a third of our smallest exporters move up a size class over five years, against 45pc in Bangladesh and 53pc in China.

Ten products dominate the merchandise basket, and it has barely diversified in two decades. This concentration has survived every exchange rate cycle; it is not a cyclical artefact, but the embedded outcome of how we allocate credit, which is through a spray and pray approach.

The correction, therefore, is not to spread money thinner across the same basket, but to point risk capital deliberately at the low base, ie the HS [Harmonised System] lines where Pakistan’s export value is small relative to demonstrated capability and global demand, and where the marginal rupee of finance changes the trajectory rather than the volume.

The targeting logic is simple to follow, ie rank the tariff lines, strip out the mature chapters that already absorb concessional finance, and identify the top 100 low-base HS codes where the constraint is financeable.

The next step is to discover those firms, and within those segments sit roughly the top 2,000 SMEs, the firms already producing, already shipping something, but stuck below the size class where banks take them seriously.

Growth in exports will not come from financing the same textile mill a hundredth time with concessional capital, but from the two-thousandth SME in the ninety-ninth HS code.

Although simply settling refunds of exporters operating at scale is also a fruit that is not just low-hanging, but actually on the ground.

Each firm can then be matched to one of three discovery pathways which can be a new geography, where an established product enters a market Pakistan barely serves; it can be a new buyer, where a firm graduates from intermediaries to direct counterparties; or a new product, where a firm scales a line from a low base.

Market entry needs 180- to 360-day facilities and certification finance, wherein buyer acquisition needs transaction-matched cover against counterparty risk, while product discovery needs 90- to 270-day working capital plus long-tenor upgrade finance. One refinance rate cannot price all three, but tailored structures can solve these problems and unlock discovery pathways.

This is where credit or trade guarantees unlock some of the value. A discovery-stage transaction fails when any one of five requirements is missing, which can be certification, a firm order, financier-grade documentation, working capital, and the plant upgrade that delivers specification.

These constraints are sequential, as the certification gates the order, the order gates the cash flow, and the cash flow gates the finance.

A partial credit guarantee, wrapped around a properly structured transaction, changes the risk calculus without replacing its judgement.

The lender continues to originate, price, and retain customers, but is more comfortable with a structured approach driven by policy and more directed towards firms actually scaling up, rather than hoping to find diamonds in the rough.

Pakistan’s food portfolio shows the method in granular detail. Pakistan’s top 50 non-rice food products earn $2.94 billion today and could quintuple to $14.7bn over five years. The binding constraints are nameable per HS code, such as quality segregation for maize, cleaning and grading for sesame, sanitary and phytosanitary and approved plants for beef, cold chain for onions and mangoes.

A granular review of data clearly suggests that processed lines already earn 31pc more per kilogram than raw ones ($0.701 against $0.535). None of these is a subsidy problem, but these are price discovery problems that can be solved through targeted capital expenditure, or working capital facilities, rather than vanilla facilities.

The decision in front of policymakers is not whether to spend more on exports. It is whether the next rupee deepens the top 100 exporters, or makes the next 2,000 firms in the next 100 product lines bankable, and scalable enough to quintuple their exports in five years. We already finance the volume, but discovery requires a structure and a thought process that does not belong to the late nineteen hundreds.

The writer is an assistant professor of practice at IBA and CEO of National Credit Guarantee Company Limited.

Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, July 20th, 2026

It is no secret that Bangladesh's non-leather footwear industry has the potential, as well as the favourable conditions, to be one of the country's great export success stories. Yet, at a time when global brands are actively diversifying their supply chains and facilitating emerging manufacturing hubs, it is unfortunate that Bangladesh has failed to capitalize on the opportunity, with export growth slowing to just 1.6% in the last fiscal year. The reasons behind this disappointing performance are both familiar and frustrating: High borrowing costs, limited access to bank financing, rising production expenses, unreliable utility services, delays in importing raw materials, and lingering political uncertainty have combined to stifle investment and expansion. While manufacturers report that demand exists, many factories are already operating at full capacity and cannot expand because financing has become increasingly difficult to obtain. This is particularly concerning because Bangladesh possesses many of the ingredients needed to become a globally competitive footwear exporter. The country has a sizable workforce, years of manufacturing experience, and growing recognition among international buyers. What is lacking, however, is an enabling business environment that allows enterprises to scale up confidently and compete with regional rivals that have captured a far larger share of the global footwear market. The government must, therefore, treat the non-leather footwear industry as a strategic export sector. Improving access to affordable finance, ensuring uninterrupted gas and electricity supplies, streamlining customs procedures, and reducing unnecessary regulatory bottlenecks should become immediate priorities. At the same time, policy-makers must provide a stable and predictable investment climate that inspires confidence among both domestic manufacturers and foreign buyers. With the right policies and timely reforms, the non-leather footwear sector could generate billions in export earnings, create thousands of quality jobs, and help diversify the country's export basket beyond garments. The window of opportunity is open, but not indefinitely -- and Bangladesh cannot afford to let another global opportunity slip away.

item.description:

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar arrived in Manila on Wednesday to participate in the 33rd Asean Regional Forum (ARF) ministerial meeting, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

“A busy programme of engagements lies ahead, including participation in the ARF plenary meeting and bilateral meetings with counterparts on the sidelines,” the FO said in a post on the social media platform X.

It said that upon his arrival, Dar was received by Elmer G Cato, the assistant secretary at the Philippines’ foreign affairs department, Pakistan’s Ambassador to the Philippines Asima Rabbani and other officials.

In a statement issued on Tuesday night, the FO said that the high-level meeting will bring together foreign ministers and delegates from 27 ARF member states, adding that the Asean secretary general will also attend the meeting.

It said that Dar will participate in discussions on “political and security issues affecting the Asia-Pacific region, with a special focus on promoting peace, stability, and mutual cooperation through sustained dialogue and diplomacy”.

He will also hold bilateral meetings with his counterpart from the Philippines and several other participating dignitaries on the sidelines of the meeting, it said.

“Established in 1994, the ARF has remained a pivotal platform for multilateral consultations on regional security issues. Since becoming a member in 2004, Pakistan has maintained an active role within the forum, consistently offering constructive contributions to its regional programmes and objectives,” the FO statement concluded.

Dar meets with Russian, Bangladesh FMs

On the sidelines of the Asean meeting, Dar met with Bangladesh FM Khalilur Rehman, who is also the president-elect of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, the FO said.

The ministers “reviewed the positive trajectory of Pakistan–Bangladesh relations and the renewed impetus by the deputy prime minister’s visit to Bangladesh last year”, the statement said, adding they reaffirmed their “shared commitment to further strengthening bilateral ties”.

The FO further said that the two dignitaries welcomed growing engagement between their countries, including “enhanced people-to-people contacts and improved connectivity following the commencement of direct flights this year”.

They agreed to sustain the “positive trajectory”, the statement added. Dar and Rehman also exchanged views on “regional and international issues of mutual interest”, the FO said.

In January, direct flights between Pakistan and Bangladesh commenced after a 14-year hiatus as an inaugural flight from Dhaka landed at Karachi Airport.

Ahead of the Asean moot, Dar met with Russian FM Sergey Lavrov in Manila.

The two leaders reviewed bilateral relations between their countries and reaffirmed their commitment to “further strengthening cooperation in trade, energy, connectivity, and other key areas, as well as enhancing coordination at multilateral forums”, the FO said.

“They underscored the importance of sustained high-level engagement in advancing the Pakistan-Russia partnership,” it added.

The two foreign ministers also exchanged views on key regional and international developments and agreed to remain in close contact.

Dar visits ADB headquarters in Manila

On the sidelines of his visit to Manila, Dar also visited the headquarters of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), where he was received by the Director General for the Central and West Asia Department, Leah Gutierrez, the FO said.

Dar signed the ADB Visitors’ Book upon his arrival. The FO said “the interaction provided an opportunity to exchange views on the ADB’s evolving development agenda, its partnership with Pakistan, and the role of Pakistani professionals at the institution”.

item.title: Kashmir, IWT among key global challenges threatening 'peaceful coexistence', Dar tells Asean moot. [ dawn ]
item.description:

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-20

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Thursday drew attention to key challenges threatening peaceful coexistence and stability across the world, listing the Kashmir dispute and India’s threats to Pakistan’s water share among them.

He made the remarks at the 33rd ministerial meeting of the Asean Regional Forum (ARF) held in Manila, the Philippines.

Foreign ministers and delegates from 27 member states of ARF gathered for the summit, which comes amid a flare-up in the war between the United States and Iran. The conflict is a key concern for the 11-nation Asean, which has a combined gross domestic product of about $3.8 trillion heavily reliant on Middle East oil.

Addressing the meeting, DPM Dar highlighted eight key challenges that he said “continue to threaten peaceful coexistence, stability and our livelihoods across the region and the world”.

“Any delay in addressing these challenges will only undermine our collective efforts to achieve peace, stability and prosperity across our regions and beyond,” he said.

Noting the “continued failure” to resolve longstanding disputes in South Asia, he particularly called attention to the Jammu and Kashmir dispute as “the heart of regional instability”.

He said that Pakistan continued to advocate for a “just and peaceful” settlement, in line with the United Nations Charter and resolutions as well as the aspirations of the Kashmiri people.

The deputy premier also expressed concern once again over India’s decision to unilaterally place the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) in abeyance after hostilities flared up between the two nations last year.

“We simply cannot afford to let this serious provocative development remain unaddressed,” Dar said, urging the entire international community to support a peaceful resolution to the issue.

The issue of water has remained a bitter point of contention between the two nuclear-armed nations since May 2025. Earlier this month, the top brass of Pakistan’s army vowed to undertake “all measures necessary” to ensure the availability of Pakistan’s rightful share of water.

US-Iran war and Gaza

Dar also highlighted Pakistan’s role in facilitating a ceasefire between the US and Iran and convening talks at the leadership level between the two arch-enemies after 47 years.

Appreciating the confidence placed in the country by the US, Iran, Gulf countries and others, he said, “These hard-earned achievements through dialogue and diplomacy have created a valuable opportunity to advance lasting peace. We must not let this opportunity slip through our hands.”

He expressed his hope that Pakistan’s efforts to bring peace would contribute to regional stability, as well as the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of normal shipping. He called on the international community to reinforce these efforts through sustained dialogue, diplomacy and constructive engagement.

Thirdly, the deputy premier called attention to the ongoing humanitarian crisis in occupied Palestinian territories, calling it “deeply alarming”.

“Our collective failure to prevent the genocidal streak unleashed in Gaza raises serious questions about our collective conscience as human beings, and about our ability to prevent the continued atrocities in the region,” he said.

FM Dar reiterated Pakistan’s support for Palestinian self-determination and the establishment of an independent, sovereign, viable and contiguous state of Palestine based on pre-1967 borders.

‘Common threat’ of terrorism

DPM Dar also highlighted the issue of terrorism, terming it “a common threat and challenge for all of us in varying degrees”.

“Pakistan has been at the forefront of the global fight against terrorism. No country outside active conflict zones has been sacrificing as [much as] Pakistan,” he said, highlighting that over 90,000 lives had been lost as well as close to $150 billion in economic damages.

Despite all odds, he said, the country was determined to fight against all forms of terrorism. He stressed that this long-term commitment required sustained national efforts and enhanced international cooperation.

In particular, he pointed out the challenge of terrorist groups operating from Afghan soil, naming the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) as groups exploiting Afghan territory to launch attacks against Pakistan.

“Pakistan has only one expectation for the Afghan Taliban regime: to not allow Afghan territory to be used for terrorism against Pakistan or any other neighbouring country,” DPM Dar said.

“If they are able to honour these commitments and fulfill their repeated promises, there will be immense opportunity for trade, connectivity and socio-economic development across South Asia, Central Asia and beyond.”

The deputy premier called on the Afghan Taliban regime and abetters of regional terrorism to refrain from allowing Afghan territory to be used in this regard, as well as urging ARF members to support these efforts.

There has been a resurgence in terrorism in Pakistan since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

Ukraine war, South China Sea tensions

On the Ukraine-Russia war, Dar expressed the country’s support for diplomatic efforts aimed at a “just and lasting peace”, saying that dialogue and diplomacy were the only path forward.

He also addressed a recent incident in the South China Sea, saying that Pakistan valued its ties with all Asia-Pacific states and urging “non-interference, restraint and engagement”.

Tension is currently simmering between Beijing and close US ally the Philippines over an incident in the South China Sea that led each to summon the other’s ambassador.

Beijing claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea via a line on its maps that cuts into the exclusive economic zones of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam, and is at the centre of long-running disputes over a multitude of islands and features.

The deputy prime minister also reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to the One-China principle recognising the People’s Republic of China as the “sole legitimate authority” over Taiwan. China claims Taiwan as its own territory, which Taiwan rejects.

Climate change

Finally, the minister addressed the issue of climate change, noting that Pakistan remained among the countries most vulnerable to its effects despite being responsible for less than one per cent of emissions.

He highlighted the country’s “ambitious” climate agenda and called for enhanced international cooperation to address what he termed a “common global challenge”.

The deputy premier called on the forum to strengthen its preventive diplomacy role by remaining “dynamic, forward-looking and focused on practical action”.

Dar welcomed the adoption of the Manila Plan of Action 2026-2036 and reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to its implementation as well as the ARF’s principles and objectives.

“As we move forward, let us renew our collective resolve to build a peaceful, inclusive and resilient region where sovereign equality, mutual respect and dialogue remain a foundation of our shared future,” he concluded.

Meetings with other FMs

On the sidelines of the ministerial meeting today, the deputy premier also held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from several participating ARF member states.

These included Oman’s FM Badr Albusaidi, New Zealand’s FM Winston Peters, Australia’s FM Penny Wong, and the United Kingdom’s newly appointed foreign secretary Ed Miliband.

Dar arrived in Manila on Wednesday. He met with the foreign ministers of Russia, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, as well as Asean Secretary-General Dr Kao Kim Hourn and the European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas.

He also attended a dinner meeting hosted by Egypt’s FM Dr Abdelatty, where the two ministers held wide-ranging discussions.

The DPM visited the headquarters of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), where he met with the bank’s Vice President (South, Central and West Asia) Yingming Yang, Vice President (Sectors and Themes) Fatima Yasmin, and Executive Director for Pakistan Nashita Mohsin.

“Established in 1994, the ARF has remained a pivotal platform for multilateral consultations on regional security issues. Since becoming a member in 2004, Pakistan has maintained an active role within the forum, consistently offering constructive contributions to its regional programmes and objectives,” the FO noted on Tuesday.

item.title: India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle

Submitted by Muheet Ul Islam on Fri, 07/24/2026 - 18:52
Paper Leak sparks student protests as anger mounts against India’s Bharatiya Janata Party
Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) hold placards and chant slogans during ongoing protests, days after thousands of protesters marched towards parliament demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, India, on 24 July 2026 (Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters)
Off

Sitting on the ground and beating a tambourine, Arya Singh was surrounded by a large crowd, mostly students, at a square in New Delhi.

“The government that is incompetent must be replaced” and “Long live the revolution”, the voices chanted in unison, led by the 18-year-old Singh.

For nearly a month, students from across the country have been gathering at Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century astronomical observatory and designated street site for protests.

Protesters are demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, and the education minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet. 

The demand comes after the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance exams, was leaked; it determines admissions into five-year undergraduate medical courses in India.

More than 2.3 million students appeared for the Optical Mark Recognition, or OMR-based exam contesting a total of 137,000 seats on 3 May.

However, an intelligence report about the paper leak through the social media application Telegram in Rajasthan forced authorities to cancel the exam, and a re-examination was held on 21 June.

Between the cancellation and the re-take, at least 12 students were reported to have taken their lives, according to an investigation by Indian Express, which reported that stress, grief and uncertainty led the students to do so. Further self-inflicted deaths have since been reported.

“Those twenty students who committed suicide had given up all outdoor activities, sports, picnics, everything, to prepare for their exams. This is not suicide, it is murder,” Singh told Middle East Eye. 

“If this had happened elsewhere, the minister would have taken responsibility and stepped down. But in India, he continues to hold on to his position without any accountability,” she added.

The ‘Cockroach Party’

The protests have been spearheaded by what is now known as the "Cockroach Janta Party", or CJP. It started as an online movement and satirical gesture after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, during an open court hearing, said that “parasites” were attacking the system and compared unemployed youth and activists to pests.

“There are youngsters like cockroaches who don’t get any employment or have any place in the profession. Some of them become media, some become social media, RTI activists and other activists, and they start attacking everyone,” Kant said. 

'They call us cockroaches, and maybe we are, because the system is decayed. What else can they expect such a rotten system to produce?'

- Arya Singh, protester

He later backtracked, saying that his remarks referred to individuals with fraudulent degrees and not to India’s youth, whom he called “the pillars of a developed India”.

His comments drew widespread anger, especially among Gen Z, who are dealing with unemployment, rising prices and growing religious divisions and communal violence after 12 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s rule. 

The movement gained further traction after Sonam Wangchuk, a well-known engineer, education reformer and climate activist from Ladakh, joined the protests in support of the CJP by going on a 26-day hunger strike that ended on 24 July.

During the last days of his strike, the 50-year-old was forcibly removed from the protest site by Delhi Police and admitted to a hospital. 

Wangchuk ended his strike after being assured that the police would no longer use force against protesters, that protesters would not face punishment, and that negotiations with the government would continue.

Singh wears the "cockroach" title as a badge of honour.

“They call us cockroaches, and maybe we are, because the system is decayed. What else can they expect such a rotten system to produce?” Singh, the protester, said. 

“The more rotten the system becomes, the more cockroaches it will produce,” she added, saying that this is why they are “out to show what happens when there is no accountability in the government.”

'Brute force'

Abhigyan, 26, a New Delhi resident who goes by one name, has been among the leading faces of the protest. He told MEE that the movement is against corruption, injustice and intolerance, and accused the government of arrogance.

'This is not the response expected from a democratic nation but from a fascist regime' 

- Abhigyan, protester

He said the BJP-led government has used “brute force” against students through lower-level party workers while senior leadership has publicly pushed narratives painting protesters as “anti-national” or as “terrorists”.

“This is not the response expected from a democratic nation but from a fascist regime, and that is what we are witnessing,” Abhigyan said.

Delhi Police, Abhigyan alleges, used sticks with iron nails to beat students, installed iron barricades with an electric current to give shocks, and used pellet guns to disperse the protest when they tried to march towards the Indian parliament on 20 July. 

The Delhi Police, however, in its post on X, termed such reports as “completely false and misleading”.

Abhigyan says there are three confirmed pellet-gun injuries while 65 people were admitted to Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, of which 15 were in critical condition.

“No person in their right mind and with faith in humanity can defend this, unless their employment depends on it or they are simply paid to defend it,” he said, adding that Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah are responsible for escalating the current crisis.

“The protesters did not have the resources to escalate the situation,” he said. 

'What kind of government is this?'

Far away from the main gathering, another group of protesters sat in a circle, reciting a poem: “Paper leak ki sankiya 80 se bhi paar hai, Kaise sarkar hai, Kaise sarkar hai,” which translates to, “Leaked papers have now crossed eighty. What kind of government is this?” 

'BJP is turning the majority of the Indian population, the youth, against them'

- Vijay Ratawal, aspiring doctor and protester

The students were referring to allegations reported in different studies that nearly 70 paper leaks of various exams have taken place in the country during Modi’s tenure.

“The use of force is making us reconsider whether the BJP should remain in power. There were doubts earlier, but now everything has turned black and white: [those] who want to benefit the common people and [those] who only want to hold the most powerful chair in the country,” Vijay Ratawal, a 21-year-old aspiring doctor protesting with the group, told MEE. 

“BJP is turning the majority of the Indian population, the youth, against them,” he said. 

The families of the protesters, Ratawal said, do not trust the system, as they have seen their dreams shatter not only due to exam leaks but also because of the implementation of policies that go against the interests of common citizens.

“The entire BJP cabinet is incompetent; they have set the country on fire on every front,” Ratawal said, citing the farmers’ protests in Gujarat, the violence in Manipur, and the tribal Chita Andolan (funeral pyre protest) in Madhya Pradesh.

“The need of the hour is to ask the BJP regime to step aside and leave the positions they hold to competent people who will serve the country without greed or lust for power,” he said, adding that the silence Modi shows is a lack of commitment to the youth of the country.

Senior citizens like Jankabi Krishnakumar Nirmohi, a 72-year-old farmer from Bhojpur in Bihar, also took part in the protests. He said that his aim was to support the ongoing protests against what he described as the “dictator mindset” of the Modi government.

“In 1974, the Navnirman and JP movements were launched against rampant inflation, food scarcity and government corruption, demanding systemic political change and workers’ rights. The intensity of those protests was much higher than this one, but the cruelty unleashed on students by the BJP government today has no parallel in Indian history,” Nirmohi told MEE. 

“When parliament loses its way, the streets begin to speak, and that is when decisions are made,” he said.

“The shamelessness of Modi can be seen in his post on X, in which he praised the education minister on his birthday while students were protesting against him,” Nirmohi said. 

“He did not even mourn the loss of the 20 students who died by suicide. The greetings and the blessing wishes show clearly where his support lies,” he concluded.

Gen Z battleground

South Asia in recent years has become a battleground for Gen Z-led protests, resulting in governments being toppled in countries like Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh. 

Sanjay Kumar, an Indian political scientist, psephologist and professor at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, or CSDS, told MEE that the youth have sent a clear signal of their unhappiness with the BJP government. 

However, he expressed scepticism about the extent to which the movement can sustain itself.

'When Parliament loses its way, the streets begin to speak, and that is when decisions are made'

- Sanjay Kumar, political scientist

“Yes, the protest is a clear indication that there is unhappiness among the youth against the current government, especially with regard to the NEET paper leak,” Kumar said, adding that opposition leaders also visited the protests in solidarity.

Kumar said he cannot confirm whether the protests were being organised by opposition political parties, as reported by sections of the Indian national media.

“My assessment is that it was neither started nor organised by opposition parties,” Kumar said. “However, once the movement began, [the] opposition saw it as an opportunity and tried to take advantage of it by sending a message to the youth that they are the ones looking after their interests.” 

But Kumar does not see a direct parallel between what is happening in New Delhi and the events that took place in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal.

“It is not useful to make such comparisons, because those are smaller countries, and something happening in the capital here has very different implications for the country,” Kumar said, 

“If you speak to people in rural areas, which make up nearly 70 percent of the population, I do not think this movement will have much resonance. The momentum is issue-specific and limited to a particular section of the population, mainly the youth of the country,” he added.

Noor Ahmad Baba, a political scientist and former professor at the University of Kashmir, believes that the BJP has not asked for the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister, because the government does not want to show any signs of weakness.

Meanwhile, Dharmendra Pradhan accused the Indian National Congress (INC), the main opposition party, of using students as political tools and disrupting the Monsoon Session of Parliament.

“Even after the government conveyed its readiness for a comprehensive discussion, the Congress chose political spectacle over democratic debate. Their objective was never solutions for students; it was disruption for political headlines,” he said in a post on X. 

“The students of India deserve far better than being treated as tools in a political campaign. They deserve certainty over chaos, solutions over slogans and responsibility over disruption,” Pradhan added. “We owe our students more than outrage. We owe them answers, reforms and accountability. That is exactly what our government remains committed to delivering,” he said.

But Baba says the government has not faced a challenge like this before and “it does not want to show any sign of weakness by asking for Pradhan’s resignation”.

“It will be interesting to see how the BJP handles this situation,” he added, saying that “having no precedent in the past does not necessarily ensure that a new precedent can’t be created.”

The government’s plan to launch door‑to‑door healthcare services is exactly the kind of proactive, people‑centred initiative Bangladesh needs. For too long, access to healthcare has depended on geography, income, and the ability to navigate overcrowded facilities. Taking essential services directly to citizens - especially the elderly, the poor, and those living with chronic illnesses - is a meaningful step toward equity. This initiative recognizes a simple truth: Many Bangladeshis do not seek care because they cannot reach it. Distance, transport costs, long queues, and lost wages keep people away from clinics until their conditions worsen. A system that waits for patients to come forward is a system that leaves many behind. As such, by sending trained health workers into communities, the government is shifting from reactive care to preventive care - and that shift will save lives. The plan also aligns with Bangladesh’s broader public‑health needs. Non-communicable diseases are rising, and early detection of diabetes, hypertension, respiratory illnesses, and nutritional deficiencies can dramatically reduce long‑term costs and suffering. Door‑to‑door services can therefore bridge these gaps, offering screening, counselling, and referrals before problems escalate. However, such an initiative only succeeds when it is implemented properly. While Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain spoke of a nationwide program, we hope that it is being piloted properly. Such a program will also be hollow if it fails to reach rural areas, urban slums, and marginalized communities. It is also evident that Bangladesh needs more initiatives with this level of ambition and outreach. In addition, for healthcare in particular, such a project, while highly commendable, cannot replace community‑based healthcare needing expansion or local clinics strengthened. Door‑to‑door healthcare can become a cornerstone of a more inclusive, resilient health system for our country, but only if it is scaled, funded, and sustained with seriousness.

item.title: How to solve groundwater depletion. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B

Bangladesh’s geography includes the extensive river deltas formed by major rivers like the Ganges and Brahmaputra, alongside a network of hundreds of small rivers. The monsoon season, occurring from June to September, contributes to 70-80% of the annual rainfall, while the dry winter months last from December to February. The annual rainfall distribution varies regionally, with the west receiving around 1,500 mm and the northeast and southeast receiving about 3,000 mm. Despite being a country with numerous waterways and adequate rainfall, Bangladesh, unusually, faces severe water-related problems in different parts of the country due to low natural recharge and high water demand. The use of surface water has been in decline due to groundwater depletion and dependence on groundwater on the rise. The problem of managing groundwater in the drought-prone northwestern Barind tract is severe, where rainfall is low. Currently, groundwater is vital for life and livelihoods, serving as the main source of clean drinking water and supporting agriculture. Approximately 90% of groundwater withdrawal is for agricultural use. In densely populated regions, the demand for groundwater often exceeds the natural recharge rates, leading to a continual decline in water levels, a situation referred to as depletion. This brings significant challenges, including dry wells, increased pumping costs, and reduced water availability for urban areas and agriculture. The situation intensifies food insecurity and water shortages, particularly as climate change results in more frequent droughts and altered rainfall patterns. Against this backdrop, addressing groundwater depletion is critical. One strategy for mitigation involves using groundwater within safe yield limits, while another approach includes the artificial replenishment of groundwater aquifers. In the Barind region, the Barind Integrated Area Development Project officially started in 1985 under the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation. It was created to revitalize the impoverished by combating severe seasonal droughts, severe water scarcity, and the need for food security. The project was reconstituted and upgraded into the Barind Multipurpose Development Authority in 1992. Groundwater issues were not mitigated and attention was given to the surface water bodies. However, groundwater problems need to be mitigated since 78% of BMDA projects rely on groundwater. Coastal regions of Bangladesh suffer from severe salinity intrusion, exacerbated by sea-level rise and reduced river flow, rendering water unfit for consumption and agriculture, alongside arsenic and bacterial contamination, leading to health crises. The managed aquifer recharge (MAR) technique is proposed as a practical solution to these groundwater issues across various regions of Bangladesh. MAR is a strategic approach aimed at intentionally replenishing aquifers with water for subsequent retrieval or enhancement of environmental conditions. This method supplements natural groundwater recharge by either injecting or infiltrating water into the ground. Various techniques are employed in MAR, including the use of infiltration ponds, injection wells, and riverbank filtration. Groundwater depletion is a significant issue in the Barind area, where the rate of decline ranges from 0.75 to 1.25 feet per year. This is exacerbated by limited natural aquifer recharge and high irrigation demands, leading to the ineffectiveness of some suction pumps. To address depletion, two primary strategies are suggested: Utilizing groundwater within safe yield limits, which requires considerable time for aquifer recovery, and enhancing groundwater recharge through artificial recharge mechanisms. Artificial recharge also offers additional benefits, such as mitigating salinity issues in coastal areas and managing water storage in urban centers like Dhaka. However, the disadvantages of MAR projects should also be taken into consideration before implementation. Implementing a MAR project necessitates a conceptual understanding of aquifer characteristics, such as the presence and type of top aquitard (clay or silt), aquitard and aquifer thickness, hydraulic conductivity, transmissivity, and specific yield. Properly designing a recharge well and assigning a recharge rate is critical; designing pumping and recharge wells involve different considerations. A low recharge rate is safer but prolongs the aquifer's recharge time, while a high rate risks clogging the aquifer, which occurs when pores are blocked, preventing adequate water flow if the rate exceeds hydraulic conductivity. Therefore, careful site specific design of recharge rates and well spacing is essential. The success of a MAR project fully depends on appropriate site specific design of the project. Water quality is also a significant concern, particularly if contaminated water is used, as it can detrimentally damage aquifers. The preferred water sources rank as follows: 1) rainwater (low contaminated), 2) pond and lake water (moderately contaminated), and 3) river water, which in Bangladesh is compromised by urban pollution. Studies indicate river water quality varies from fair to marginal, with high levels of sulphate and contamination risks like arsenic and salinity. Thus, river water must be treated to remove contaminants before it can be safely injected into the aquifer. Dr. Mohammad Abul Fazal is a specialist in agricultural engineering. He achieved his PhD in groundwater management from Kyoto University, Japan.

The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to renew Volker Turk’s mandate as high commissioner for human rights for four years despite strong opposition from the United States, Russia and Israel.

By a vote of 144 in favour, 10 against, and 13 abstentions, the assembly approved the renewal, beginning October 12, 2026, as proposed by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

An alternative proposal from Russia to extend the mandate by only a few months, until December 31, 2026, was overwhelmingly rejected, as was the US request to postpone the vote.

Ambassador Jeff Bartos, US representative for UN management and reform, criticised the four-year renewal on both procedural and substantive grounds, accusing Guterres of having rushed the process.

“Make no mistake: If this assembly tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts, there will be consequences.

“The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding,” he warned just before the vote, accusing Guterres of having rushed the timetable “to hand his long-term friend a four-year executive payout”.

French Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, however, described Turk as “a voice of conscience” who had demonstrated “rigour and impartiality” during his first term.

Turk, an Austrian jurist, has served as high commissioner since October 2022. He has emphasised the universality of human rights and the need to apply international law equally.

During his tenure, he has been outspoken on the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the war in Gaza, Afghanistan, Sudan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nicaragua.

But he’s also been criticised for not taking more decisive positions on Cuba, the plight of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, China, and for not directly using the word “genocide” in reference to Gaza, unlike several UN experts and rapporteurs.

Turk’s stances have earned him sharp criticism from several governments, notably Russia and Israel.

Both nations’ ambassadors voiced opposition Friday to his renewal, saying Guterres, whose term as secretary-general expires at the end of the year, should have left the selection of the human rights commissioner to his successor.

item.title: Does the government have a concrete plan for child safety?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B

Last month, in my opinion article, “ Child Safety: Beyond Ideological Polarization ,” published in the Dhaka Tribune, I argued that the sexual abuse of children -- including cases occurring within madrasa settings -- is fundamentally a structural governance challenge rooted in weak accountability mechanisms, regulatory failures, and institutional neglect. The urgency of this argument has become even more evident in recent days. Disturbing content has been circulating on TikTok, featuring madrasa teachers openly sexualizing and objectifying their child students. Accompanied by provocative comments, this trend reveals a deeper social crisis: The normalization of predatory attitudes toward children and the total absence of effective preventive safeguards. It forces us to confront an uncomfortable question: Why do these educational institutions continue to fail to ensure child safety, and why does the state allow it? To answer these questions, we must look beyond surface-level moral failings and examine the institutional architecture within which these abuses occur. Bangladesh’s response to child protection crises remains trapped in a reactive cycle. After every tragedy, public anger intensifies, demands for justice peak, and political leaders offer swift sympathy. Following the heartbreaking Ramisa case, the prime minister’s visit to the victim's family and commitment to justice provided necessary, immediate reassurance. Such gestures matter, but they cannot substitute for the institutional systems required to prevent abuse before it occurs. Before the election, the prime minister repeatedly assured the public, " I have a plan ” for the nation. We must now ask for the procedural details of the plan regarding the protection of children. We can no longer afford institutional silence, nor can we accept abstract promises. The current crisis demands a coordinated national response. The government should initiate immediate cross-sector collaboration to develop a concrete, actionable child protection roadmap. This roadmap cannot remain a policy document alone; it must address the deep, internal layers of madrasa management -- including labour standards, teacher residency rules, child protection training, independent monitoring, complaint mechanisms, and external oversight. Most importantly, the roadmap must answer practical questions: How will children be protected tomorrow? How will the educational institutions be monitored? What mechanisms will ensure absolute accountability? A plan on paper is not a plan in practice. The true measure of leadership is not how effectively it responds to public outrage after harm occurs, but whether it builds institutions capable of preventing abuse in the first place. Our children deserve more than sympathy after they suffer; they deserve a system designed to protect them before tragedy strikes. Aisha Siddika is a PhD Candidate at McMaster University, Canada.
